title: Root-cause and fix the long-rollout NaN
objective: Explain why backpropagation through the long MLS-MPM rollout returns a NaN even though the forward loss stays finite, and find a fix that lets optimization continue cleanly past the failure point.
findings: The NaN is a float32 overflow, not a mathematical singularity. Near-zero grid-mass nodes (mass as small as 1e-12, present at 511 of 512 steps) make the grid step's backward pass, which scales like 1/m, amplify the gradient by up to 1e12. Once such a node coincides with one carrying real loss-gradient, the signal overflows the f32 ceiling and becomes NaN. Three independent results confirm it: f64 runs clean (270 orders of magnitude more headroom), longer horizons fail earlier, and a no-contact center target fails earlier than a wall target (ruling out wall contact). The fix is mass stabilization, dividing by max(m, eps) with eps=1e-4, which caps per-step amplification at 1e4. The stabilized 512-step f32 run completes 100 iterations with zero NaN and reaches loss 9.5e-6, far past the old failure point. Full derivation in the failure-modes textbook section.

results.caption: Mass-stabilized 512-step f32 run: 100 iterations, no NaN, loss reaches 9.5e-6.
Stabilized optimization reaching the target with no gradient blow-up.
Horizon sweep: longer rollouts fail earlier (the fingerprint of long-rollout amplification)
Precision: f64 has the headroom f32 lacks (overflow, not singularity)
Contact isolation: the no-contact target fails earlier, ruling out walls
